hints: Look carefully at the words polypeptide, molecule and fibre in B and C, collagen has a clear hierarchy and they are not interchangeable.
Remember why glycine appears every third amino acid in collagen and what type of bond actually holds the three chains together.
walkthrough:
**Recall the levels of collagen structure**

Think small to big. Three collagen polypeptides wind together to make one collagen molecule (the triple helix). Many molecules then pack together to make fibrils and fibres.

So: 3 polypeptides = 1 molecule, many molecules = fibre.

**Check the special amino acid and bonding**

Collagen has Gly-X-Y repeats, so about every third residue is glycine. Glycine has the smallest R group, just a hydrogen atom ($R = H$), so the three chains can pack very tightly together.

The three chains are held to each other by hydrogen bonds and cross-links, not by peptide bonds. Peptide bonds only join amino acids within a single polypeptide chain.

**Pick the correct description**

Option A correctly describes the high glycine content and its tiny R group. The other options mix up polypeptides with fibres, confuse collagen helices with alpha helices, and confuse hydrogen bonds with peptide bonds.

options.A: Correct. Glycine occurs every third residue and its very small R group allows the three polypeptides to coil tightly into the triple helix.
options.B: Incorrect. It is three collagen polypeptides (not fibres) that coil to form the triple helix, which is one collagen molecule.
options.C: Incorrect. Collagen polypeptides form a left-handed helical coil, not regular alpha helices like those in many globular proteins.
options.D: Incorrect. Peptide bonds join amino acids within each chain, while hydrogen bonds (plus cross-links) hold the three different polypeptides together.
